# Independent review of the smallest field generated by a power

<a id="abelian-power-intersection"></a>
## The field intersection and the finite families

At 2026-11-17T09:05 UTC an agent outside proof development reviewed the [fixed submission](../../claims/Yin_C_G0345_v195.md#decision-abelian-power-intersection-submitted) for Sheng Yin.
The reviewer received the statement and proof without development discussion, author explanations or previous conclusions about this submission.
The proof establishes the field intersection, the classification including both estimates in (3), and the claimed sharp orders of growth.

Compressing the support exponents by their gcd \(g\) gives a monic polynomial that must be irreducible because substitution preserves any nontrivial factorization.
Its root \(\beta=\alpha^g\) therefore has degree exactly \(1/g\) times the degree of \(\alpha\), which cancels the factor \(g\) in its height.
Substitution preserves the coefficient length of a relation at \(\beta\).
Conversely the degree \(g\) of \(\alpha\) over \(\mathbb Q(\beta)\) forces every residue-class polynomial of a relation at \(\alpha\) to vanish at \(\beta\).
At least one such polynomial is nonzero and its coefficients are a subset of the original coefficients, so taking minima gives the reverse inequality.

For each \(n\), the extension of \(L=F(\alpha^n)\) obtained by adjoining \(\alpha\) is the splitting field of a separable binomial.
Its automorphisms fix all \(n\)-th roots of unity, so the quotient \(\sigma(\alpha)/\alpha\) is an injective character and \(\gamma=\alpha^{[L(\alpha):L]}\) is fixed.
Writing \(r=[L(\alpha):L]\), the minimal polynomial of \(\alpha\) over \(\mathbb Q(\gamma)\) has degree at least \(r\) by extending scalars to \(L\), and at most \(r\) by the binomial.
Hence \(p_\gamma(X^r)=p_\alpha(X)\) by divisibility and equality of monic degrees.
It follows that \(r\mid g\), so \(\beta\in L\) for every \(n\), including when \(r=1\).
At \(n=g\) the lower field is itself one of the fields in the intersection; at every multiple of \(g\) the reverse inclusion follows by powering \(\beta\).

The retained rational-base height bound applies to the infinite abelian field \(F\) and the nontorsion point \(\beta\).
In particular the retained reduction to a finite abelian field containing the minimal-polynomial coefficients preserves the relative degree; the source's discriminant prefactor is not set to one.
The degree follows by dividing the common measure by the height bound.
Multiplication of the root factors bounds the coefficient sum by \(2^{\deg p_\beta}e^{m(\beta)}\), and \(p_\beta\) is itself an admissible relation.
For \(\delta\le D\) the maximum of \(H\) on the integers \(1,\ldots,D\) is finite, giving bounded integer coefficients and bounded degree for the seeds.
Normality of \(F/\mathbb Q\) makes the relative degree the same at every conjugate seed root.
Conversely an irreducible substitution from the list satisfies both bounds and recovers its exponent \(s\) as its support gcd, and therefore recovers its unique seed.
An arbitrary positive power has absolute degree at least its relative degree over \(F\).
Consequently, if the measures stay bounded and the minimum relation lengths tend to infinity, the absolute degrees tend to infinity uniformly over all positive powers, as asserted for the cited conditional construction.

For fixed degree and seed there is at most one substitution exponent, with irreducibility both necessary and sufficient.
Summing this bound once for classes and with a factor of the degree for conjugates gives the two cumulative upper bounds.
For the proposed example, every \(K\)-conjugate of \(\phi^{1/s}\) has the same modulus, so the absolute value of the relative norm is the positive unit \(\phi^{e/s}\) in \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)\).
If \(0<e<s\), this unit \(u=\phi^{e/s}\) lies between \(1\) and \(\phi\), and its trace \(u+1/u\) or \(u-1/u\) lies strictly between successive integers in either case.
Thus \(e=s\); the tower law gives \(2s\) distinct conjugates and proves the displayed polynomial is minimal.
The root has \(s\)-th power in the quadratic abelian field and its measure is \(\log\phi\).
Summing these distinct classes over the even degrees gives both lower orders.
The review used the retained Amoroso–Delsinne theorem at its stated scope; it did not re-audit the source's determinant or ramification proof.
